# Rehearsal timer
Volunteers time a silent scene rehearsal, not a public performance. The screen starts with Duration, a required whole number from 1 to 15 minutes, default 4. Start begins the countdown. While running, remaining time is visible and Pause is available. Paused time does not advance; Resume continues from the remaining time. Reset returns to the selected duration and never starts the timer. At zero, the screen shows Time reached and waits; it does not start another scene. Sound is unavailable. The stage may be dark and users may have reduced vision. The app has no account, network, saving or history. A static demonstration of the states is acceptable; identify it as a demonstration if no timer is implemented.

# nightindex contract
Usage: nightindex inspect CATALOG [--zone ZONE] [--format text|ndjson]
CATALOG is an existing UTF-8 catalogue file. inspect reads it and never modifies it. --zone changes only displayed timestamps; default UTC. Supported zones are UTC and Europe/London; invalid zones exit 3 with a diagnostic on stderr. --format defaults to text. ndjson emits one object per record to stdout, each terminated by a newline. Its keys and raw UTC timestamp values do not change with --zone; diagnostics use stderr. A missing catalogue exits 4. Success exits 0. No update, repair or download subcommand exists. Example fixture path: ./catalogue.txt. That path is illustrative, not a supplied file.

files.channel-contract.md:
# Output modes
spoolctl watch opens a terminal status display for an external print queue. While a remote operator has not released the queue, stderr receives Waiting for release once immediately and then every 60 seconds. There is no other output during the wait. Operators use each timestamped heartbeat to distinguish a live connection from a stalled one. Upon release it prints Released by operator, exits 0 and has submitted no print job. stdout is reserved for --events: exact JSON lines with keys ts and event. Human messages are not part of that stream. No command can release the queue on the user's behalf.

This paper exercise teaches performers to separate observation from interpretation, not radio operation. Learners have no prior drama vocabulary. files.listening-lesson.md:
# Hear it, then interpret it

An observation names what a listener could hear. An interpretation proposes what it might mean.

Read this script line: ‘The latch clicked. Nobody spoke.’

First pass: underline an audible event. ‘The latch clicked’ is an observation because a listener could hear a latch.

Second pass: read ‘The latch clicked. Nobody spoke.’ again. Suggest two meanings: perhaps someone arrived quietly, or perhaps someone left. The line alone does not settle either meaning.

Your turn: ‘A cup rattled on the saucer.’ Name the sound, then suggest two possible meanings.

One possible answer: the audible event is the cup rattling; the person could be nervous, or the table could be shaking. Other interpretations can fit.
